title: Ruzzco Barbers POS & Forecasting
description:
My BSIT capstone at Systems Plus Computer College: a point-of-sale and sales forecast for Ruzzco Barbers in Caloocan. I'm the lead developer on a five-member team.


## The problem

The shop records sales in paper logbooks. That makes it hard to credit each sale to the right barber, settle commissions, count the drawer at day's end, or plan ahead.


## What I built

- Offline-first POS: barbers record sales on assigned phones. Sales are saved on the phone first (IndexedDB) and sent to the server when the connection returns. Each sale is validated on its own, so one bad sale never blocks the rest, and retries never create duplicates.
- Money handling: every sale is attributed to the barber assigned to that phone at the time of sale, and commissions are saved with the sale. There is an end-of-day cash reconciliation and a barber payout ledger, plus an owner dashboard. PayMongo QR payments run in test mode with safeguards against charging a sale twice.
- Forecasting: a FastAPI and scikit-learn service predicts daily customer counts from digitized logbook records, and revenue is derived from that.


## The key decision: fix attribution at sale time

Phones can be reassigned between barbers. Tying each sale to its assignment, not to whoever holds the phone now, means a reassignment can never rewrite past commissions.


## Forecasting result

I compared Random Forest with simple baselines over four held-out weeks (Oct 2–29, 2026). Random Forest averaged 5.2 customers/day of error. The simple average scored 5.2, a weekday average 4.7, and a naive baseline 4.4. With only about a month of test data, the simple baselines were as good or better, so I report that and don't claim the model wins.

## What I'd change

- Gather requirements more thoroughly. I moved into building before I fully understood how the shop actually runs.
- Show the client working software every sprint. Our paper uses an incremental, iterative SDLC, but iteration without periodic client feedback is just a series of builds. I should have demoed updates regularly and acted on what the owner said.
- Say so when something isn't right. I knew the v1 front-end design wasn't up to standard. I kept it so the effort behind it wouldn't be wasted, and it became the biggest critique of our system design. Being non-confrontational cost the project more than an honest conversation would have. Next time I raise the issue early, even when it's uncomfortable.
tech_stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Prisma, MySQL, Dexie (IndexedDB), FastAPI, scikit-learn, Docker
summary: Capstone project: an offline-first point-of-sale and customer-count forecast for a Caloocan barbershop. I led a five-member team.

title: Loc-it
description:
LOC IT was created as a bonus deliverable for our challenge during the Henkel Philippines Hackathon 2026.

While our main campaign proposal focused on #LOCINWITHLOCTITE, LOC IT served as a practical demonstration of how the campaign could extend into a digital consumer experience—helping consumers discover the right LOCTITE product, understand why it fits their needs, and find a path toward purchase.

The prototype was developed within the hackathon timeframe as a concept demonstration, rather than as a production-ready commercial platform. Visit in https://github.com/rhbntm/loc-it to see more details
summary: A LOCTITE product-finder prototype built as a bonus deliverable for the Henkel Philippines Hackathon 2026.

title: JR Inventory Management System
description:
A stock and pricing system I built for my friend's ukay (secondhand clothing) live-selling business. The owner used it on his phone to count and price incoming batches.

## The problem

In November 2025 my friend started live selling, with him hosting on camera and me running the backstage as admin. Everything ran on paper: when a buyer commented "mine" on an item, I wrote their name on paper tape, stuck it on the item, and screenshotted the comment as proof.

Paper kept up during the live, but not after it. Matching claims to checkouts took 15–30 minutes, and how much stock was left was a guess. New batches were worse: supplier counts are only estimates, so every batch was tallied in a notebook and each item was priced by hand with the owner's formula.

## What I built

- **v1 (Laravel + Filament, Nov 2025):** built during a one-week exam break and in use by day 3, on a laptop.
- **v2 (Next.js, Prisma, PostgreSQL, Docker on a VPS):** a phone-first rebuild. To count a batch, the owner picks up each item, checks it for damage and price tier, and taps +1 (or +1 "damaged"). When the batch is counted, the system applies his pricing formula to every item.

## The key decision: phone-first

The owner wasn't using v1. His laptop was slow and he isn't technical, so instead of adding features, I moved the system onto the device he already used every day. That change is what got him using it.

## Result

Batch counting replaced the notebook, and pricing went from hand calculation to automatic. After-live reconciliation got faster too, though most of the value came from batch intake.

The system is no longer in daily use. The business moved from ukay to regular stock and stopped live selling, so the workflow it was built around went away.

## What I'd change

- **Find the cause before rewriting.** v1's slow page loads came from my own development setup, not from Laravel. Next time I'd profile first.
- **Design around the real user from day one,** not after he stops using it.
- **Expect the process to change.** The system encoded one workflow, grading secondhand items, and stopped fitting when the business did.
content: This is my first project using React and Supabase.
summary: A stock and pricing system for a friend's ukay (secondhand clothing) live-selling business, used on a phone to count and price incoming stock

title: My portfolio
description:
This site is my portfolio and the custom CMS behind it. I manage posts and projects from a protected admin panel instead of editing code.

### Key Features

* Markdown editor with live preview, drafts, and drag-and-drop image uploads with compression.
* Supabase for the database, authentication, and image storage.
* A daily GitHub Actions job that mirrors published content and images to the repository.
* An automatic fallback to that mirror, so public pages stay readable if Supabase is unavailable.
content: A responsive task manager with drag-and-drop features, reminders, and real-time syncing across devices.
summary: My portfolio and its custom CMS: an admin panel for posts and projects, backed by Supabase with a daily GitHub mirror as a fallback.
